slides.title: Our Home: Earth, a Unique Life Sustaining Planet
slides.subtitle: Of perhaps billions of planets in the universe, Earth is the only one we know where life, as we know it, exists and thrives in all its forms.
points: What do you think Earth would look like if there were no life on it at all?
Life on Earth has survived for billions of years — what allows it to keep going despite major changes and disasters?
Why don't dogs lay eggs? Or hens give birth to live chicks?
If a spaceship carried soil and water to Mars, could plants start growing there?

slides.title: Why is Earth a unique planet?
slides.intro: While there are perhaps billions of planets in the universe, Earth is the only one where life thrives. Let us begin by seeing just how thin the layer of life really is.

slides.title: Life clings to a wafer-thin skin
slides.body: All the mountains, rivers, forests, animals, and people are found on a **very thin layer** on the surface of our planet. From the tallest mountain to the deepest ocean trench, the **crust** — where all of life exists — is tiny compared to the size of Earth. If Earth were the size of an apple, the crust would be no thicker than the apple's **skin**. This delicate, life-supporting layer is what makes Earth truly special.

slides.title: List the features we take for granted
slides.purpose: We want to notice the everyday features of Earth that we usually overlook, but that quietly make it special — so we list out what makes our home unique.
steps: List — some features of Earth that we take for granted but are interesting and important to us
Recall — the air we breathe doesn't fly off into space (Chapter 7: gas particles move freely, gases have no fixed volume)
Recall — we can stand on the ground held by gravity (Chapter 5), yet our heart can still pump blood up to our head
Discuss — your list with your teacher and friends
slides.observe: Earth is interesting and important in many ways — it provides the **air** we breathe, the **water** we drink, the **soil** that grows crops, and materials like **rock and timber**. It is a unique planet that not only allows life to exist but **sustains** it.

slides.title: What do the planets of our solar system look like?
slides.intro: Our solar system has eight planets going around the Sun in nearly circular orbits. Let us compare them and ask why the planet closest to the Sun is not the hottest.

slides.title: Eight planets, only one with life
slides.body: Eight planets orbit the Sun in nearly circular paths. In order of increasing distance from the Sun, they are **Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune**. Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars are relatively **small, rocky** planets; Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune are **large** planets made mostly of gases. Out of all these, only Earth — so far — is home to life.

slides.title: Compare temperature, size, and atmosphere
slides.purpose: We want to test a simple idea — that planets closer to the Sun should be hotter — by collecting real data on each planet, so we gather the facts and look for the surprise.
steps: Collect — information about the temperature and size of the planets, and whether they have an atmosphere
Use — books in your school library, trusted websites, or discuss with your teachers
Fill — the missing information in Table 13.2
slides.observe: All planets get their energy from the Sun, so we expect them to get **colder** the farther they are. This is mostly true — **except Venus**, the second planet from the Sun, which has the **highest** average temperature and is the **hottest** planet. Why is this so?

slides.kicker: TABLE 13.2 · PLANETS IN OUR SOLAR SYSTEM
slides.title: Closer isn't always hotter
Why Venus beats Mercury for heat
slides.body: Venus is the hottest planet not because it is closest to the Sun, but because its **thick atmosphere traps heat**. The air on Venus is almost entirely **carbon dioxide**, which does not let the heat escape — this is the **greenhouse effect**. On Earth too, gases like carbon dioxide trap heat by absorbing the radiation given off by the warmed Earth. This greenhouse effect plays an important role in maintaining **just the right temperature** on Earth.

slides.title: What makes the Earth suitable for life to exist?
slides.intro: Earth's special conditions come from where it sits, how big it is, and what shields it. Let us look at its position, its size, and its magnetic field.

slides.title: Position of the Earth
slides.intro: The single most important reason Earth can support life is its distance from the Sun — just right for water to stay liquid.

slides.title: Earth sits in the Goldilocks zone
slides.caption: The band of distances from a star where water can stay liquid — the habitable, or 'Goldilocks', zone.

slides.title: The right distance keeps water liquid
slides.body: Earth is at **just the right distance** from the Sun for the temperature to allow **liquid water**. Closer, and it would be too hot and the water would evaporate; farther, and it would be too cold and the water would freeze. Liquid water is essential for life to evolve. The range of distances around a star where water stays liquid is the **habitable zone**, or **Goldilocks zone**. So much of Earth is covered with water that, seen from space, it looks blue — hence the name **Blue Planet**.

slides.title: Did Mars ever support life?
slides.body: Mars lies at the **edge** of the Sun's habitable zone. Several spacecraft have been sent and rovers have explored its surface, but **no proof of life** has been found yet. Scientists think that in the past Mars may have had **liquid water** — maybe even lakes — and conditions that could support simple life forms. This is one reason Mars still interests scientists, and a reminder that science doesn't always have final answers — it stays open to change as we learn more.

slides.title: Size of the Earth
slides.intro: Distance from the Sun isn't the only factor. Earth is also the right size — to hold on to an atmosphere without crushing us.

slides.title: Not too small, not too big
slides.leftBody: If Earth were much smaller, its gravity would be too weak to hold on to the gases in our atmosphere, and they would escape into space. On Mars the atmosphere is **100 times thinner** than on Earth, and Mercury has no atmosphere at all.
slides.rightBody: If the planet were too large, gravity would be so strong it could pull us down with such a large force that our **bones could get crushed!** Earth's size is just right to hold an atmosphere, which is essential for life.

slides.title: Oxygen breathes — and shields
slides.body: The presence of **oxygen** in Earth's atmosphere lets us breathe and is needed by almost all forms of life. But oxygen has another important role: some of it gets converted into another form called **ozone** (a three-atom oxygen molecule), forming the **ozone layer**. This layer acts like a **shield**, blocking harmful **ultraviolet (UV) rays** from the Sun that can damage living cells.

slides.title: Magnetic field of the Earth
slides.intro: A freely suspended magnet always settles in a fixed direction — because Earth itself behaves like a giant magnet. That magnetism turns out to be a shield too.

slides.title: A magnetic field guards us from space
slides.body: Earth behaves like a **giant magnet** — it is believed that the movement of **molten iron** in Earth's core is the origin of its magnetic field. Earth is constantly hit by tiny, high-energy particles from space: those from far across the universe are **cosmic rays**, and those from the Sun are the **solar wind**. These can damage the atmosphere, reduce the ozone layer, and let in more UV rays. Thankfully, Earth's magnetic field acts as a **protective shield**, pushing many of these harmful particles away and keeping our atmosphere — and life — safe.

slides.title: What allows life to be sustained on Earth?
slides.intro: Earth has the right conditions for life, but it is the beautiful connections between living and non-living things that let life thrive. Let us explore how air, water, soil, and life interact.

slides.title: Air and water keep life going
slides.body: The atmosphere holds **oxygen** for respiration, and in sunlight plants take **carbon dioxide** from the air and water from the soil to make food by **photosynthesis**, releasing oxygen. Water is essential for life: it covers about **70 per cent** of Earth's surface — in ponds, lakes, rivers, seas, oceans, and groundwater — and all this water forms the **hydrosphere**. Water vapour in the air forms clouds and brings rain or snow, refilling rivers, lakes, and underground water.

slides.title: The geosphere supports everything
slides.body: Beneath our feet lies Earth's crust, made of **rocks, soil, and minerals**. It provides almost everything life needs — soil to grow plants, and minerals that give us salt, coal, oil, and metals like iron and copper. The solid parts of Earth are known as the **geosphere**. Soil may look like simple dirt, but it is rich in nutrients like **nitrogen and potassium** that plants need, formed by the slow breakdown of rocks and the remains of plants and animals. The variety of landforms, soils, and rocks, with the processes that shape them, is called **geodiversity**.

slides.title: All of life makes the biosphere
slides.body: Earth is full of life — from trees, shrubs, and herbs to animals, insects, and tiny organisms invisible to the naked eye. All living beings, along with the places where they live, make up the **biosphere**. As you learnt in Chapter 12, living beings depend on one another: plants make food through photosynthesis, animals eat plants or other animals, and **decomposers** break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil. Nature works together as a **system** to support life.

slides.title: Everything works together
slides.body: Earth is like a giant **teamwork project** between nature, weather, and life itself. It is a vast, balanced system where land, air, water, and living things support and affect one another. Even a **small change** in one part — like cutting down a forest — can impact rainfall, soil, air quality, and the animals that live there. Life survives not because of any one thing, but because everything works together in **balance**. That is why protecting clean air, water, soil, and all forms of life keeps our planet healthy for the future.

slides.title: What keeps life from disappearing?
slides.intro: If plants and animals didn't reproduce, life would eventually disappear from Earth. Reproduction ensures each kind of organism continues — and lets life change over time.

slides.title: Parents pass on the instructions
slides.body: Animals usually produce young that resemble them — cows have calves, cats have kittens — because parents pass on **instructions** about how to develop from a single cell. These instructions, called **genetic material** or **genes**, are stored inside every cell, like a detailed instruction manual. But reproduction does more than copy: small changes in the instructions can help a plant or animal survive better — like camels developing **humps** to store fat in deserts. Over generations, such changes lead to new features, and even new types of living beings.

slides.title: Asexual reproduction
slides.intro: In asexual reproduction, a single parent produces new individuals that are exact copies of itself.

slides.title: Grow a new plant from a part
slides.purpose: We want to see how a single plant part can grow a whole new plant on its own — vegetative propagation — so we plant cuttings and watch life begin without seeds.
steps: Take — a stem cutting of a money plant, the 'eyes' of a sprouted potato, or a piece of ginger
Plant — each one separately in moist soil (not too deep); a money plant cutting can go in a glass of water to watch easily
Watch — every day, and note how many days it takes for roots, stem, and leaves to appear
slides.observe: A whole new plant grows from just a **part** of the parent — leaf, stem, or root planted in soil. This is **vegetative propagation**, a kind of asexual reproduction where one parent makes individuals that are **exact copies** of itself. Bamboo and sugarcane grow this way, with no seeds at all.

slides.title: Planaria regrows from a fragment
slides.body: Not just plants — microbes and simple animals also reproduce asexually. Single-celled organisms like **bacteria** and **amoeba** divide into two identical individuals. Algae can regrow from small cut parts, and **Hydra** grows tiny **buds** that break off and become new individuals. **Planaria**, a type of flatworm, can regrow from a single **fragment** of its body — scientists study it to understand regeneration in animals.

slides.title: Sexual reproduction
slides.intro: In sexual reproduction, two parents — usually male and female — are involved, and their genes mix in new ways each time.

slides.title: Gametes carry half the instructions
slides.body: If both parents passed on all their genetic material, the child would end up with double the instructions, doubling every generation. This doesn't happen because each parent makes specialised reproductive cells called **gametes**, which carry only **half** of the parent's genetic material. When male and female gametes join, they form a new cell with a **complete** set of instructions — half from each parent. Because each gamete carries a different mix, every child is **unique**: one may inherit a nose like the mother, another eyes like the father.

slides.title: How gametes meet
slides.leftBody: **Pollen grains** in the **anther** are the male gametes; **ovules** deep inside the flower are the female gametes. Pollen is carried by wind, insects, or animals — **pollination**. When gametes combine — **fertilisation** — a **zygote** forms that becomes the seed, and the flower's fleshy part develops into fruit.
slides.rightBody: Gametes are called **sperm** (male) and **eggs** (female). In fish and frogs, fertilisation happens in **water**. In birds and mammals, sperm are deposited inside the female's body. Birds **lay** the fertilised egg and the embryo develops while it is incubated; in most mammals the embryo develops **inside** the mother's body.

slides.title: What are the threats to life on Earth?
slides.intro: Life on Earth depends on a delicate balance of living and non-living things. But human actions are disturbing that balance — even small changes can put life at risk.

slides.title: Burning fossil fuels traps extra heat
slides.body: Normally, Earth keeps its balance as trees, plants, and even tiny ocean **planktons** absorb carbon dioxide as they grow. But burning fossil fuels like coal and oil releases greenhouse gases like **carbon dioxide and methane**, plus extra carbon that was locked underground for millions of years. Earth cannot absorb it fast enough, so heat builds up. Even a small temperature rise can melt **ice caps**, raise sea levels and flood coastal cities, and cause extreme weather. These long-term changes in temperature, rainfall, and weather patterns are called **climate change**.

slides.title: Three threats, one disturbed balance
slides.body: When habitats are destroyed, plants and animals disappear, upsetting ecosystems — if grasses vanish, deer and grasshoppers struggle, and predators lose their food too. **Pollution** of air, water, and soil from factories, vehicles, and waste harms people and nature. Together, these are the **triple planetary crisis**:

slides.title: The world agreed to act
slides.body: Countries have made global agreements to protect the environment. The **Montreal Protocol (1987)** helped reduce chemicals like **CFCs**, letting the **ozone layer** slowly recover. The **Earth Summit (1992)** drove global efforts on climate and biodiversity, and the **Paris Agreement (2015)** committed countries to cut greenhouse gas emissions, aiming to limit global warming to below **1.5 °C**. But as of 2025, the world is not on track to meet that goal — much more action is needed.

slides.title: Protect our unique planet
slides.subtitle: All the Earth systems are connected, so damage to one affects the others. Cleaner energy, less waste, reusing and repairing — sustaining life on Earth needs everyone, from local communities to global leaders.
